heading: Can't Stay With a Feeling?
after: Further reading: D’Antoni et al., 2022 — Comparative study of EMDR, Brainspotting, and related methods
before_heading: Layer 4: Unstick the Memories You Can Actually Point To
paragraphs: If, as soon as a feeling starts in a session, you're already explaining where it comes from, or agreeing with whatever the therapist says so the moment will pass, [Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy](https://psykologtidsskriftet.no/debatt/2021/09/intensive-short-term-dynamic-psychotherapy-methods-evidence-indications-and) would say it's anxiety about the feeling that makes you slip away like that. In that therapy, the therapist points it out as you do it and keeps pushing for the feeling, while watching for signs of that anxiety, like tense muscles, sighing, or your thinking going foggy, to tell when it's getting to be too much for you. If you can only take a little of it, like most people who try this therapy, you'd get a slower version, where the therapist stops to help you settle whenever the anxiety climbs.

If it's one feeling in particular that scares you, like grief, [Affect Phobia Therapy](https://psykologtidsskriftet.no/node/15971/pdf) treats that fear a lot like a phobia, getting you used to the feeling bit by bit, at a pace your anxiety can handle.

And if what you can't let in is kindness, when someone cares about you and it just bounces off, there's [Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy](https://www.apa.org/pubs/videos/4310759). The therapist works to keep you from feeling alone with whatever comes up, and when some of their care does get in, they ask what that's like and where you feel it in your body.

All three keep steering you back toward your feelings, which can get to be too much. So before booking, I'd ask the kind of thing I'd ask a water therapist: "What happens if I get overwhelmed, or if you say I'm dodging a feeling and I don't think I am?" I'd want them to say they'd slow down, and that they'd listen.

heading: Imagery Rescripting
after: While EMDR is often treated as a therapy for anyone with trauma
paragraphs: This therapy is a lot like the way I [re-do trauma memories](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/i/189761959/re-do-trauma-memories) in my inner child reparenting guide. Instead of EMDR's mechanical approach. The Imagery Rescripting therapist is there with you as you explain the scene, and they step in as the ideal adult, protecting and nurturing your inner child. Then you learn to do that yourself. Because rescripting takes you back into the memory like EMDR does, the same care goes for it: stop when it's too much, and ground yourself afterward.

From [a trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32892758/) on 155 patients, it looks like it works on average about as well as EMDR, although that doesn't tell us if it works better or worse for you or anyone else.

heading: Pain That Won't Quit?
after: Inner-child reparenting is another form of integration therapy
before_heading: Optional High-Intensity State-Shift and Release Practices
paragraphs: If your pain has lasted months, and a doctor has checked and found no injury or disease to explain it, two therapies are worth knowing about. In the first, [Pain Reprocessing Therapy](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8482298), you learn to treat the pain as a false alarm. It's real, but it's your brain signaling danger where the doctors haven't found any injury. Part of how you learn that is by paying close attention to how the pain feels in your body without fearing it. Then, a little at a time, you go back to things you've been avoiding because of it, like going for walks.

Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain. There, 66% of the people who got four weeks of the therapy rated their pain 0 or 1 out of 10 afterward, compared to 20% of those given a placebo shot, and the gains mostly held a year later.

The second therapy is for pain that seems bound up with stress and feelings about the people in your life. [Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03918642) works on the feelings directly. Much of the therapy is letting out anger and other feelings you've held back, and rehearsing in role-play what you'd say to someone you've never stood up to.

In a 2024 trial of veterans aged 60 and up, this therapy beat CBT: 63% had their pain drop by at least 30% afterward, compared to 17% with CBT. A 30% drop is a lower bar than getting your pain down to 0 or 1 out of 10, so the two trials' numbers can't be compared.

I haven't found a trial comparing the two therapies. So if your pain seems tied to stress or to people in your life, I'd start with the second, and otherwise with the first. I'd also ask a therapist where they trained in that therapy, and keep track of how it's going the way I describe in the last section, [How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping](#§how-i-judge-whether-any-of-this-is-helping).
